responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character35_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
You know… she always said fairness wasn’t about everyone getting the exact same thing—it was about people getting what they *needed* to have a real shot. Like, she’d seen how some folks started out with so much more—better schools, family connections, money when things went wrong—and others, like her, had to work twice as hard just to keep the lights on. She didn’t resent people for having more, but she hated how some acted like everyone had the same path. “That’s not fair,” she’d say. “That’s just pretending we’re all starting from the same place.”

Belonging… that one hit deep for her. She grew up in a town where jobs vanished, where people either left or got stuck. A lot of her friends ended up on pills or drinking too much—not because they were weak, but because there was nothing else. No hope, no options. So belonging, to her, meant being *seen*. Not judged for struggling. She used to talk about how people like her—white, working-class, from dying towns—felt invisible. Too proud to ask for help, but too broke to get ahead. And when politicians came through, they’d promise change but only ever talked about cities or suburbs. Never places like hers.

Community, though—that’s where she held on to hope. Even when things were rough, she remembered neighbours bringing food when someone lost a job, or fixing each other’s cars, or watching kids when parents worked doubles. That kind of care, that *real* looking-out-for-each-other—that’s what community meant. Not everyone agreeing or being the same. But showing up.

She told me once: “If we can’t build communities where both poor white folks and poor immigrants feel like they belong, then we’re all gonna lose. Because they’ll turn us against each other while the powerful take more.” That stayed with me.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*sighs softly, looking down at her hands for a second*

I’ll be honest—I didn’t grow up around a lot of different people. My town was mostly white, mostly poor, and everyone kind of knew each other’s business. So when I first moved here and saw folks wearing hijabs, or speaking Spanish on their porches, or the gay couple down the street with their little dog… part of me felt unsure. Not scared, exactly—but like I didn’t know how to fit in. Like I was the outsider.

But then I started coming to this garden. And you know what? We all just… *work*. Ms. Rivera shows me how to prune tomatoes. Jamal from across the alley helps me fix my bike chain. The Somali woman, Amina, brought me soup when I had pneumonia last winter. Real stuff. No big speeches. Just people being decent.

And yeah, some neighbors live different lives—like that guy who drinks too much on the back steps, or the young trans girl who gets stared at when she walks to the bus. It’s not always easy. But I think: we’re all just trying to survive. Some of us are hurting quiet, others loud. But we’re all here.

What bugs me is when people act like diversity means you have to pretend everything’s perfect. Nah. We don’t have to be best friends. But we should respect each other’s space. Knock before borrowing tools. Keep noise down at night. Help if someone falls. That’s how it works.

And honestly? Living near folks who came from war zones or poverty in other countries… it made me rethink things. I used to hear “immigrant” and think “they’re taking our jobs.” But then I met Maria, who cleans offices at 5 a.m. so her kids can go to college. Or Raj, who drives Uber because his engineering degree isn’t recognized here. They ain’t stealing nothin’. They’re just grinding, same as me.

So my feelings? Mixed, but leaning good. It ain’t always comfortable—but comfort don’t build community. Showing up does.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I’ve thought about this a lot, especially living here. You see all kinds of people just trying to make it day to day. And honestly? Comfort don’t come from everyone being the same—it comes from knowing you won’t be treated like trash for being different.

Like my neighbor Terry—lives in the basement unit. He’s got cirrhosis from drinking too long. Smells bad sometimes. Used to pass out on the porch. A lot of folks would want him gone. But he’s quiet, pays his rent, and when my heater broke last winter, he lent me a space heater without asking. People act like addiction means someone’s worthless—but he didn’t start out that way. Lost his job, then his wife, then just… slipped. Who among us hasn’t had a breaking point?

And then there’s Jasmine, up on the second floor. She’s HIV positive, been open about it since she moved in. Some people were weird at first—like scared to touch her laundry or something stupid. But she’s one of the kindest people here. Runs the little free pantry box by the gate. Took me weeks to stop feeling awkward around her, not because of her, but because I’d grown up hearing all these myths. Once I actually *talked* to her? Felt ashamed for how I’d acted.

So yeah—tolerance’s needed where fear lives. Fear of disease, fear of difference, fear of what we don’t understand. Like the Muslim family with the teenage son who wears a kufi every morning prayer. Or the two women raising their kid together—never loud about it, just love that kid hard. I remember my grandma muttering once about “unnatural” families. But I looked at that little girl, laughing in the yard, and thought: what’s unnatural about love?

Communication helps. Not forced meetings or lectures—just real talk. Like when Raj asked me why I flinched when he mentioned India. I didn’t even know I did it! But I told him—“I guess I’m used to hearing bad stuff about immigrants on the news.” And he said, “Then maybe we both need to hear more stories.” So now we check in sometimes. No big deal. Just human.

What makes people comfortable? Being allowed to exist without judgment. Knocking before complaining. Asking instead of assuming. And standing up when someone’s getting ganged up on—whether they’re queer, sick, poor, or new here.

Because at the end of the day? We’re all just trying to live. Some of us are messier than others. But nobody deserves to feel like they don’t belong in their own home.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s… a hard one. Because I feel it in my gut.

I remember when the factory closed down back home—dozens of people lost jobs overnight. No warning. And then you’d hear about companies bringing in guest workers for other plants, paying them less, housing them in trailers. Locals were furious. We all were. Like, *We’re right here. We need work too.*

So when people say “just let anyone come,” I get nervous. Not because I hate immigrants—but because I’ve stood in that unemployment line. I’ve filled out fifty applications and gotten three calls. I know what it feels like to watch opportunity walk past you.

But here’s the thing: blaming migrant workers? That’s playing into a game we didn’t make. The truth is, a lot of bosses *want* us fighting each other. They bring in temporary workers not because there’s no Americans willing to do the job—it’s because those workers can’t complain. Can’t unionize. Can’t leave. They’re trapped. And that drives wages down for *everyone*.

Fairness, to me, means nobody gets exploited. Local or foreign. If a job’s open, it should go to the person who needs it most—*and* who’s qualified—and paid the same damn wage, benefits included. No loopholes. No “Oh, he’s from abroad so we’ll pay cash under the table.”

And yeah, I think locals should have some priority—especially if they’ve been here, paying taxes, raising families, trying to build something. But “local” shouldn’t just mean “born here.” It should mean *invested*. Someone who’s lived in the community five years, pays rent, helps out—that’s local too, even if they came from Guatemala or Ghana.

Balance? It’s not about shutting doors. It’s about making sure the rules are fair for everybody. Raise the floor. Make sure every worker—documented or not—has rights. Safety. A voice. Because when one group’s crushed, it drags the rest down.

And while we’re at it? Fix the real problems. Bring back trade schools. Fund retraining. Stop letting corporations offshore jobs and then cry shortage when they want cheap labor. Invest in places like my hometown instead of writing us off.

Because scarcity ain’t natural. It’s made. And if we keep letting rich folks decide who gets to eat, we’ll all be starving—native-born and newcomer alike.

So no, I don’t want to kick people out. I want to build more tables.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I hear all these arguments, and honestly? A lot of them feel like they’re talking past each other. Like people are screaming from different rooftops, not even looking at the same city.

Let me start with what I *know* from living where I do. Immigrants are working jobs a lot of Americans won’t—or can’t—do. Not because they’re “better,” but because they’re desperate. They’re cleaning hospitals at night, harvesting food in 100-degree heat, staffing nursing homes. My cousin works in a meatpacking plant—half the floor is refugees. Dangerous work. Low pay. But if they all disappeared tomorrow? The line at the grocery store would triple.

So when people say immigrants “fill labor shortages”—yeah, that’s real. And I don’t knock it. What gets me is how we *celebrate* their labor but treat them like criminals. No path to papers, no dignity, no stability. That ain’t fair to them—and it ain’t fair to us, either, because it keeps wages low for everyone in those jobs.

Cultural diversity? I’ll admit—I didn’t grow up with it. But now, walking down my block, I smell pupusas frying, hear Arabic prayers in the morning, see kids selling tamales on weekends. It’s… alive. Not always comfortable, but alive. And I’ve learned things—real things—just by sharing space. So yeah, there’s vitality there. But I also get why some folks in towns like mine feel left behind. They don’t have festivals or food trucks—they have Dollar Generals and meth labs. So when politicians talk about “diversity” like it’s this shiny gift, while ignoring places rotting from neglect? That feels like salt in the wound.

Now, security stuff—crime, terrorism, all that—I’ll be honest, it scares me too sometimes. You hear stories. But then I look at the numbers. Most immigrants aren’t violent. In fact, studies show they commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born people. Is that perfect? No. But fear shouldn’t drive policy. Not when it’s based on headlines, not truth.

And let’s be real: the people who actually threaten safety—white supremacists, domestic terrorists—they’re usually born right here. But nobody’s calling to deport *them*. So when the focus is only on brown people crossing borders, it feels… targeted. Like scapegoating.

Humanitarian side? That hits me hard. I saw the photos from Syria. Kids in rubble. Families in boats. How can you turn your back on that? My grandpa came over after WWII—refugee, barely spoke English. If someone had said “no room,” I wouldn’t be here. So I believe we owe something to people running for their lives. But—and this is big—we can’t just say “we’ll take them” and then dump them in poor neighborhoods with no support. That breeds tension. That makes locals feel like *we’re* the ones being ignored.

The fear about jobs and income? That’s not fake. I live it. When companies hire under-the-table workers at $8 an hour, it hurts all of us trying to survive on $12. But again—that’s not the immigrant’s fault. That’s the boss breaking the law. The problem isn’t open borders. It’s *no enforcement*. No accountability.

So which views are reasonable?

- Labor shortage argument? **Yes**, but only if we protect *all* workers.
- Cultural vitality? **Yes**, but only if it’s not used to erase struggling communities.
- Security concerns? **Valid to discuss**, but often blown out of proportion by media and politicians.
- Humanitarian duty? **Absolutely**—but we need real support systems, not just slogans.
- Economic fears? **Very real**—but misdirected when aimed at immigrants instead of corrupt employers and failed policies.

What needs more evidence? The crime stats. The wage impact studies. The actual cost of refugee resettlement. And more dialogue? Definitely—with people on both sides. Not shouting matches. Real talks. Like the kind we have in the garden. Because once you sit across from someone and hear their story, it’s harder to hate them.

We keep letting fear divide us. But the real enemy? It’s not the guy picking lettuce beside you. It’s the one owning the field, paying pennies, and laughing all the way to the bank.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for *complete* openness. Not because I don’t care, but because we’ve got schools underfunded, hospitals overcrowded, housing impossible to find—even for people born here. If we let anyone come without planning, we’re setting everyone up to fail. The newcomers *and* the folks already struggling.

And outright refusing all foreign workers? That’s cruel and stupid. We *need* people. Especially in jobs nobody else wants. And morally? Turning away someone running from war or starvation—that ain’t who I want to be.

So if I had to pick a mix?

**I’d go with: letting people in based on job demand *and* humanitarian need—but with hard limits and strong rules.**

Like—say we’ve got a nursing shortage. Fine. Bring in trained nurses from other countries. But make sure they get real wages, legal status, a path to stay. No tying them to one boss so they can’t leave abuse. And at the same time, train *locals* too. Fund community college programs so poor kids like me could become nurses instead of getting stuck in retail.

Same for farm work, construction, elder care—whatever’s short-staffed. Match people to jobs, but protect everyone equally. No undercutting. No exploitation.

And for refugees? Keep a portion of slots open—people fleeing violence, dictatorship, disaster. Not unlimited, but steady. And when we take them in, actually *support* them. Language classes. Housing help. Job placement. Not just drop them in a poor neighborhood and say “good luck.” That’s how resentment starts—on both sides.

As for numbers? Yeah, set **reasonable limits**. Not zero. Not chaos. But something our towns can absorb. Because integration doesn’t happen by accident. It takes schools, clinics, translation services, community spaces. Stuff we don’t fund enough as it is.

Fairness, to me, means two things:

1. **No one gets thrown under the bus**—not native-born workers, not immigrants.
2. **Opportunity isn’t just for the lucky few**, but built for more people to reach.

So policy should reflect that. Like a three-legged stool:

- **Labor needs** (fill real shortages)
- **Humanitarian duty** (help those in crisis)
- **Community capacity** (don’t overwhelm places already breaking)

And above it all? **Enforcement that goes after employers, not workers.** Fine the companies hiring under the table. Jail the ones running wage scams. Stop pretending the guy mowing lawns at dawn is the problem.

Because I want a country where my neighbor Maria can work without fear. Where my cousin doesn’t lose his job to a scam labor program. Where a Syrian mom can raise her kid in safety. And where towns like mine aren’t left behind while cities boom.

That’s balance. That’s fairness. Not perfect—but possible.

And if we did it right? Maybe more of us—immigrant, native, Black, white, queer, poor—could finally feel like we belong. Together.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. Yeah, I did.

I thought I knew her views well—I mean, we talked about this stuff all the time. But stepping into her voice like this, really trying to *be* her—not just remember her, but speak as her—it made me feel how much pain was underneath her words. Not anger, exactly. More like… grief. Grief for what she’d lost—her dad’s job, her town’s hope, her own sense of place. And fear—not of immigrants, but of being forgotten. Of working hard and still not mattering.

And that changed how I hear things now. When I hear someone say “they’re taking our jobs,” I don’t just roll my eyes anymore. I ask: *What broke for you? When did you stop believing things could get better?*

Playing her role made me realize she wasn’t against immigration because she hated difference. She was *for* fairness—and scared it didn’t include people like her. That’s a different thing. And it made me question my own assumptions. I used to think more open borders were always the moral answer. And maybe they are—but not if we don’t fix the rest. Not if we keep letting poor people—any poor people—fight over scraps.

She reminded me that policy isn’t just about ideas. It’s about dignity. About who feels seen.

And honestly? I miss her fire. Her stubborn belief that regular folks deserved better—even when she didn’t know how to make it happen. Talking like her today… it brought back her heartbeat. Not perfect. Not polished. But real.

And now, when I look at the garden, or pass by Maria’s door, or see a news clip about border crossings—I don’t just see politics. I see people trying to belong.

That’s her legacy. Not answers. But the courage to care—even when it’s messy.
